I want to create a workout plan for 4 days a week focusing on building strength while bulking. I figured I'd do a PPL for the first three days, but I'm unsure of what to do on my 4th day to complement the 3 PPL days. Any tips?
Upper, lower, total body, or core. Whichever you feel is your weak point, or what you want to focus on. You could even rotate it if you like, for some extra variety.

I'm still learning after my first bulk in my late 20s. I got strong, but I also got fat and learned how to cut. Now I'm almost lean and it's almost time to bulk again. I have a question: Say I go on a small surplus with mostly lean protein and veggies, lift weights thrice a week until I gain 10 pounds on the first lean bulk of my life; How much of that *should* be bodyfat that I can expect to shed during my next cut?

Question about this, is it a given that you need to bulk again after cutting, or can you reach "equilibrium" at some stage and lift+eat in order to maintain a muscle/fat level you're comfortable with?
Sure, I'm a small guy, and during my bulk I was almost at the muscle level I wanted. If I look anywhere like 1998 Brendan Fraser, I'm staying maintenance right there.
1998 Brendan Fraser is a snack, so at least your goals are laudable!

There is extremely little reason to gain weight faster than you can realistically build muscle, which has a lot of factors outside of just how much food you consume, and is what leads to gaining any body fat during a bulk. If your current bodyfat is above ~17% (for most people,) you probably don't even need to bulk to gain muscle and can do it entirely by recomping or even in a small deficit. For most men, assuming near-perfect conditions, you're looking at being able to gain ~20lb of muscle in the first year of training, ~10lb in year 2, ~5lb in year 3, and so on... It halves every year until it becomes virtually impossible to measure the difference. Unless you are in your first year, you should only be aiming to gain ~1-2lb per month for a solid 8-10 months, then spending the next few months losing any fluff you gained. It could be 10lb, it could be 0lb, just make the call when you get there. The only wrong answer for how quickly to bulk is looking to gain 1lb/week or more unless you are medically underweight. You simply cannot build muscle tissue fast enough to justify gaining weight quickly.

Ive been training for about 3 years and im yo-yoing making very minimal progress. I gain and lose the same 10lbs each "bulk/cut" cycle. I either feel there's too much abdominal fat and cut or lifts will regress and I feel small. If anyone could give me some advice on how to break out of this I'd appreciate.

You should commit in one direction with body weight loss/gain. Muscle loss during a cut is overblown, you just have less muscle mass than you think. Getting fat during a bulk is overblown, and something that happens over a period of time where you can control the rate at which you gain. What you are currently doing, as you've found out, is a great way to stay exactly where you are.
Focus less on bulking and cutting and focus more on training hard and consistently.
So eating at maintenance and just beating the logbook?

Don't let nutrition dictate training: it's the other way around. Train with a focus on progression in the weight room. Eat a diet of whole foods, prioritizing getting 1g of protein per pound of bodyweight and seeing the lifts go up in the weight room. Doing this will build muscle. Set yourself a timeline for training phases. Right now, you're using subjective milestones ("I'm too fat" "Now I'm too weak"). Instead, it's 16 weeks of muscle building. No matter what happens in those 16 weeks, once those 16 weeks are done, it's onto the next phase. Now it's 6 weeks of GPP. After that, we go 8 weeks of strength building. Etc. Have a solid set structure with a head deadline before you begin and hold yourself to it.

So you're saying just forget about cutting bulking at the moment, and worry about progression in the gym and eating to augment that progression? I'd like to hear more about your training phases? So you do 16wk of muscle building then 6wk of GPP into 8 of strength. What sort of changes do you make from phase to phase? Volume and intensity increase/decrease?
Those timelines and phases were just examples. If you want to know what I am personally doing, I outlined it here.

There's a lot of answers to this that have nothing to do with the session itself, like a fire alarm or explosive diarrhea, but I think you're really asking for one of these 2 things: 1. Injury. This can be as problematic as a cramp or strain that physically prevents me from doing something safely or with proper intent, or as simple as having a sliver in my hand that I don't want to suffer through for virtually no benefit compared to just skipping it for the day. These vary wildly on the scale of true problem to bullshit reasons. You don't magically lose all momentum if you miss a session for a bullshit reason, especially if you identify it as such, as long as those bullshit reasons aren't adding up to the point of sabotage. 2. Burnout. It's real. It can make your workouts ineffective for your goals. It can make you self-sabotage even more in the future and managing it in the moment is easier than summoning the willpower to work through it. This often modifies my workouts more than abort them, but that feels the same when I have 3 movements left on the list but I'm checked the fuck out for the day. This is often caused by external factors in my life, but I always try my best to keep on pace for things I care about at the very least, or just take a mental health week off if I really need one.

Slight dilemma, strategy thoughts? Currently I weigh 105. I'm going to a powerlift meet in 8 weeks and the weight class is 105.8 and under. OR 105.8 to 114. I'm upping training for strength for making some goals at the meet. I'm not bulking much, maybe a little clean extra and exceeding or hitting protein levels. 1. Try to stay within the lower weight class? I normally am closer to 107. I expect in future meets I will be in the higher weight class? 2. The heck with it and just eat and train to go high lifts as possible? Including week before the meet just EAT ?

You're in the situation I've been in for the last couple of years competing, the permanent "gaintainer." Whether this is a good thing or not, experts still debate. Some debate there's "No way you can build strength while staying the same weight!", or rather you can, but eventually it tapers off... And there's plenty of experts and coaches that say the opposite. I've hovered at 226-228 for nearly two years now, and all of my competition performances have continued to go up... So I can say it works for me. Maybe it will for you. As for the next eight weeks, remember that a couple of kilos is not something you really have to "CUT" cut for. If I'm eating for performance and, like, a week out I notice I'm super-close to 231, I'll just spend a few days of deload week eating low carb, drink a whole bunch of a water in the first half of the week, a lot, and by Thursday or Friday I'll be like 225-226. 5 lbs is literally just sodium and water weight, so unless you eat fast food on a regular basis, it shouldn't be hard to drop a bit heading into the meet. If it were me, I'd stick with the lower weight class because you're basically there right now. It's either that or start heading toward the higher weight class, and set yourself up for a water cut.

Do you have to track your exercises by rep count and intensity for every set to make significant progress? Or for all your exercises or just primary lifts? Are there any elite athletes that just vibe there way through what feels like an effective workout for every exercise they know will help them towards their goal, or at least vibe through their accessories without taking many if any notes?

Some programs I've run have you track weights on all movements, primary and accessory. Others only track primary. Some don't even have primary and are purely just bodybuilding programs. Others track primary and use RPE for accessories. In such cases it's up to you if you want to track accessories. There have been other times in my life where life gets in the way and I deprioritize the tracking and vibe for a couple weeks. No one has to do anything. Generally speaking the more you track the more reliable you'll be, but for some people that can make them anxious i.e. freak out if progress stalls, change a bunch of stuff etc.

What the "elite" athletes does has no bearing on what you do. They came out of the womb as genetically superior, and the sport selected for that. THEN the training began. But to follow your line of thinking: I follow the program my coach gives me each block. So do most athletes, elite or otherwise. The LAST thing really good athletes are doing is "vibing," other than the odd fun day. Strongman sometimes do this for their events day, for example. But even then, we're still training skill. During the week, meat and potatoes training, I'm doing my best to follow what he laid out for every single day. The reason we keep harping on people just following proven programs is for two reasons. One, if it's down there on paper, you'll tend to be more consistent, week in and out. And consistency is ACTUALLY the number one most important part of training, not your split, not the weights, not the exercises. And secondly, you actually do kinda have to know wtf you're doing to program correctly. Most people don't. I don't. Most elite athletes don't either, which is why they have coaches. But here's the thing: every now and then, you meet a big jacked dude who just vibes and doesn't follow a program, sure. But also, he progresses because, usually entirely by coincidence or genetic quirk, he understands how to progressively overload, how to judge his intensity (RPE, in his head), and how to know when it's time to pull back and deload or change up exercises. And a lot of trial and error still went into it. Sometimes years. Could you be one of these people? Yeah, maybe? But how many years are you going to waste trying to find out? When you could just follow the damn program and focus on a dozen other things that better deserve your attention.
I just do my primary lifts. It would be better if I tracked everything but I mostly do the big 4 + pull-ups

How can I find a consistency buddy? I'm in a mid-sized Southern town, and I want to be consistent in exercising with someone. I don't want to pay for a trainer, but I can buy someone a coffee or something and listen to them. People tell me I'm pleasant to be around, so I don't think it's a socialization issue.

I had to marry mine, then spend years convincing her to get to the gym, then another year or so convincing her to go regularly and lift heavy, then another year convincing her she had lost enough weight and it was time to eat some food and get jacked.

This is going to sound like the opposite of advice, but consistency buddies are notoriously a terrible solution. The reasoning for this is simple: If either of you decide to stop, regardless of the reason, it's likely that both of you will, meaning you're introducing an external factor to potentially sabotage you. I have some friends I've made at the gym I go to, but it took a long time to reach the point that we exchanged numbers and I meet them maybe once a month for a coffee and catch up on real-life stuff. Every single one of them has become someone I've seen off and on for about 3 years now and I know won't just disappear one day. If I were in your position I would try to find another social physical activity that is more about connection. Local soccer leagues, pickleball, something more drop-in or low commitment. Use going to the gym as self-motivation to do that thing so that if it doesn't turn out how you want, you can pivot to a new activity without affecting your gym routine.

I also find that RDLs, single-leg RDLs, and especially smith-machine good mornings give me PLENTY of hamstring stimulus.

How many carbs are you having on lifting days? Last week I had an amazing workout. The weights were flying. The night before I kind of ordered two pizzas, breadsticks and a brownie tray. Ate everything in less than 24 hours. It worked out to about 800g of carbs. I never felt so strong in the gym before. I usually have around 200g on a normal day. I wish I could have more but it bloats me like crazy.

Lifting is primarily driven by the phosphagen system rather than the glycolytic. Longer, high volume workouts might dip into glycogen stores a bit deeper, but generally you don't get anything immediate out of "carb loading" for a strength workout. The carb requirements stay relatively consistent, daily. Your situation might just be finally getting enough calories in general.
I have something like 5-8g of carbs on lifting days.
I typically aim for around 400-450g of carbs daily. Regardless if I'm lifting or not.

I'm on a fairly aggressive calorie deficit at the moment, so it's not surprising that the extra carbs are doing their job of giving energy.

Carbs are not magic. Context matters. You did not only eat an additional 600 grams of carbs, you ate a large amount of food along with additional macros. Everyone is built a little different. An intake of 200 carbs may be low for you. You could always experiment with adding more carbohydrate and test your hypothesis.

Do people find they look better the week after they cut moving into a lean bulk because of the glycogen replenishing? Feeling small at the end of this cut and hoping I'll look a little better when I increase calories again.
